items.prompt: importBackup runs JSON.parse(text) as ExportData. When a malformed backup file is loaded, what does the 'as ExportData' part actually do?
items.answer: Nothing at runtime, as the cast is erased and code may read fields the file never had
distractors: It throws a TypeError at parse time as soon as a required ExportData property is missing
It strips unknown properties during parsing, so only the declared ExportData fields survive
It coerces field types to match the interface, turning numeric strings into real numbers
items.explanation: TypeScript types are erased at compile time - the cast produces exactly the same JavaScript, which is why a separate runtime validator has to exist at all.

items.prompt: validateImport is declared with 'asserts payload is ExportData' rather than returning a boolean. What does that signature buy?
items.answer: The result can't be ignored, as it throws or returns, and after a return the payload's type is narrowed
distractors: The whole check moves to compile time, so no runtime validation cost remains in the shipped bundle
The function may repair the payload in place, filling in defaults, before the caller continues using it
It lets the bundler tree-shake the validator out of production builds once types are checked
items.explanation: A boolean validator can be called and its result dropped; an assertion function makes that impossible - a bad payload never gets past the call site.

items.prompt: The day helper checks a YYYY-MM-DD regex, that Date.parse is finite, AND that re-formatting the parsed date equals the input. What does that third check catch?
items.answer: Rollover dates like 2025-02-30, which parse into March, so the re-formatted string differs
distractors: Timezone offsets that would shift an exported date by one day when it is formatted back to ISO
Two-digit years such as 25-02-28 that slip past the four-digit regular expression check
Dates before the Unix epoch, whose negative timestamps make toISOString return a different day
items.explanation: Date.parse('2025-02-30') is a valid timestamp in V8. Only formatting back to 2025-03-02 and comparing against the input exposes the impossible calendar date.

items.prompt: A backup contains two review states for the same cardId, each individually well-formed. What happens on import?
items.answer: It is rejected as 'Malformed backup: review state': a Set of seen ids trips on the repeat
distractors: The later state wins: put() overwrites by primary key and the file is processed in order
Both are written: Dexie's ConstraintError then aborts the transaction after the clear
The duplicate is silently filtered out: a state for an unknown card is dropped in the same way
items.explanation: Catching duplicates in validation matters downstream: bulkAdd would otherwise throw a ConstraintError mid-transaction - safe, but it would reject the file with a far more confusing error.

items.prompt: importData validates the payload before the transaction AND replaces all four tables inside one transaction. Why are both layers necessary?
items.answer: Validation stops bad data before storage is touched; the transaction covers quota errors or crashes
distractors: The transaction exists purely for speed, as Dexie commits batched writes faster than single ones
Validating inside the transaction would deadlock Dexie's readwrite lock held on the four tables
Either alone would suffice; pairing them is redundant defense in depth, kept around for the reviewers
items.explanation: Validation alone leaves you exposed to non-data failures; the transaction alone would let well-formed garbage in. Each guards a failure class the other cannot see.

items.prompt: Inside importData the callback calls reviewStates.clear() and then bulkAdd(states). What makes that destructive sequence acceptable?
items.answer: Both run in one readwrite transaction, so any failure after clear aborts and restores the tables
distractors: clear() returns a snapshot of the deleted rows that bulkAdd uses to roll back on an error
The validator guarantees bulkAdd cannot fail once clear has succeeded, so no rollback is ever needed
Dexie defers the deletes in clear() until the callback returns, so nothing is lost on failure
items.explanation: Outside a transaction, a failure after clear() would leave the user with no progress at all - the guide calls this out as the reason the transaction is load-bearing, not decorative.

items.prompt: A backup from an older build references card ids this build no longer bundles, and says nothing about newly added cards. How does import handle both?
items.answer: States and logs of unknown cards are filtered, and missing bundled cards get fresh states
distractors: The file is rejected, as every card id in a backup must match the current bundle exactly
Unknown states import as orphans and are garbage-collected at the start of the next session
Unknown states are filtered, and newly added cards stay stateless until they are first reviewed
items.explanation: Cards ship with the app, so id drift across builds is expected - filter, don't fail. The regression test pins all three behaviours: kept progress, omitted unknown logs, recreated states.

items.prompt: Unknown CARD ids in a backup are dropped on import. What happens to an unknown DECK id in settings.enabledDeckIds, and why does nothing break?
items.answer: It is kept: deck ids just need to be strings, and its counter just stays empty
distractors: It is dropped: the same known-ids filter removes it along with states for unknown cards
It fails validation with the 'Malformed backup: settings' message and nothing is imported
It crashes the stats screen later: that screen looks every enabled deck up by id
items.explanation: A deliberate asymmetry worth noticing: card ids are domain-checked, deck ids only type-checked. Whether to drop stale deck ids too is left as exercise 3.

items.prompt: The validator accepts ease 1-10, yet the scheduler never drops ease below 1.3 and 'Easy' adds 0.15 with no upper clamp. What lesson do the guides draw from this mismatch?
items.answer: Rules not derived from the producer accept values the app cannot emit, and may reject ones it can
distractors: The validator must be loosened to accept any positive ease value, so older backups keep importing
The scheduler is buggy and should clamp ease to exactly 10 so it can never exceed the validator
The mismatch is exploitable, as imported cards with a high ease can skip their reviews
items.explanation: ease 1.0 is accepted though unreachable; ease 10.15 is theoretically reachable (after decades) and would be rejected. Neither crashes - the point is the gap between 'a validator exists' and 'the validator matches the domain'.

items.prompt: Before bulkAdd, importData strips the id field off every imported review log. Why?
items.answer: Logs use auto-increment keys, so file ids could collide with keys Dexie assigns to later reviews
distractors: The validator has already rejected any log that carries an id, so stripping it is only defensive
Dropping the ids shrinks the stored rows, which noticeably speeds up a large backup import
Dexie refuses bulkAdd whenever any primary key is supplied explicitly in the added rows
items.explanation: Fresh keys for appended history, stable keys for keyed rows (settings, meta) - the destructuring { id: _id, ...rest } is the one-line version of that policy.

items.prompt: A backup arrives with schemaVersion 2 while the app is at 1, and the validator rejects it - newer and older alike. Why is that the honest choice today, and what replaces it when the format evolves?
items.answer: With no migration code, other versions have an unknown shape; later, migrate step by step, then validate
distractors: Newer versions should import unchanged, as fields are only ever added; older ones need the migrator first
Dexie's version().stores() chain already migrates backup files, so the check is only a safety net
The validator should warn and accept instead, as schemaVersion is advisory metadata in a backup
items.explanation: The backup file's version and IndexedDB's schema version are two separate systems - rejecting unknown file versions is the only claim the code can currently back up.

items.prompt: After each rejected import, the regression test re-exports the database and deep-compares states, settings and meta against the original. What failure mode does that second half guard against?
items.answer: Code that writes first and validates afterwards, where a rejection-only assertion would still pass
distractors: Flaky ordering between Dexie's async rejection and the test runner's own await on the import promise
Mutations leaking between test cases through the shared original fixture that each case clones
A validator that throws the wrong error message even though it rejects for the right reason
items.explanation: Checking the rejection proves the error path exists; comparing the stored bytes proves 'a bad file changes nothing' - which is the actual invariant the change promises.

items.front: DevDeck import design (src/db.ts:166-201): validate the whole backup first, then clear-and-refill four tables in one Dexie transaction. State the guarantee this buys and the two gaps the decision note concedes.
items.back: Guarantee: a bad file changes nothing, and a failed write leaves previous progress intact. Conceded gaps: the error names only the failing block, never the record, and nothing checks that settings refer to decks that actually exist.

items.front: validateImport(payload: unknown): asserts payload is ExportData (src/importValidation.ts:3-5). Why take unknown, and why the asserts form instead of returning true/false?
items.back: unknown forces every property to be checked before use - the compiler never saw the file's bytes. The asserts signature makes the check unskippable: it throws or returns, and only a normal return narrows the type, so a bad payload cannot travel past the call.

items.front: saveReview puts the updated review state and adds the log inside one transaction (src/db.ts:118-126). What inconsistency does this rule out?
items.back: Stats can never show a review whose state change was lost, or a state change with no log: both rows commit or neither does. It is the import's all-or-nothing idea applied at the scale of a single graded card.

items.front: validateImport stops at the first problem, reports only the block name, and caps arrays at 100,000 states / 1,000,000 logs (src/importValidation.ts:21-34). What is each choice trading away?
items.back: Block-only messages mean a user with 2,000 logs learns one is bad but not which one - cheap to write, poor to debug. The size caps exist to stop a huge file from freezing the tab, not because real data approaches them; both are deliberate scope cuts, not oversights.
